title: Loose at the Foot
passage:
A pair of gates does not shut flat across the chamber. The leaves meet in a shallow V pointing up the canal, and the pair is longer than the lock is wide, so the water above presses the joint closed instead of forcing it open. Each leaf pivots on a heel post rounded by hand, and the post stands on a pin in a cup set in the stone. The pin is not fastened down. Nothing down there is fixed against a sideways push, so the water shifts the leaf what little it can and beds its heel into the iron plate that lines the recess. The push runs along the leaf into the masonry, and next to none of it reaches the pin. What the pin carries is the weight of the leaf. The collar at the head of the post gets shimmed too, but that is a matter of hang, of the mitre posts meeting true. Green oak throughout, and measured in feet and inches, because that is how the lock was cut.
– Duncan Thurlmede, lock carpenter

questions.prompt: What are we told about the pin the leaf stands on?

options.text: Nothing anchors it, so the leaf can settle and bed its heel firmly against the wall iron.
It is fixed hard into the stone so that the leaf cannot move once the water rises.
It carries the leaf's weight, which is usually why the collar above it has to be shimmed.
It takes the whole of the water's push, and every leaf is hung to make certain of it.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, key_derivation paraphrase_one_sentence, anchored on the six-word verdict sentence and the long sentence that follows it: 'The pin is not fastened down. Nothing down there is fixed against a sideways push, so the water shifts the leaf what little it can and beds its heel into the iron plate that lines the recess.' A recasts exactly that - the foot is unanchored, and that freedom is what lets the leaf seat its heel against the iron in the wall - in different words, and adds nothing the text does not supply. The next sentence corroborates it from the other end: 'The push runs along the leaf into the masonry, and next to none of it reaches the pin.' B is the reversed mechanism and the strongest pull on a solver who has not read carefully: every hinge a reader has ever met is bolted down, so a gate holding back a canal ought to be bolted down hardest of all. The passage refuses it in its shortest sentence - 'The pin is not fastened down' - and the refusal is load-bearing, because a fixed foot would intercept the push that the text sends into the masonry. C is a half-right conjunction, and the option a careful-but-hasty reader stops on. Its first clause is true and stated almost in those words: 'What the pin carries is the weight of the leaf.' The second clause then glues on a cause the passage assigns elsewhere - the collar 'gets shimmed too, but that is a matter of hang, of the mitre posts meeting true' - so the shimming is about how the gate hangs, not about what the pin bears. The 'usually' adds an unsupported frequency claim on top of that; nothing in the text says how often collars are shimmed. D is the quantifier upgrade, built on the passage's own account of where the push goes: it absolutises 'next to none of it reaches the pin' into its opposite extreme, the pin taking 'the whole' of the water's push, and bolts on a second absolute ('every leaf is hung to make certain of it') that the passage never states. Hedge balance: the key is a flat, unhedged assertion; the only hedged option (C, 'usually') is wrong and the only absolutiser (D, 'the whole ... every') is wrong, so neither 'pick the qualified answer' nor 'strike out the absolutes' locates the key. Lengths under mech tokenisation: A 17, B 17, C 18, D 19 - the key is tied for shortest and is never the longest option, ratio 1.12 against the 2.36 ELF cap.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: PHYSICS CHECK, run 2026-08-26 BEFORE drafting, because batch15's TYPE-001 short was refuted at V-FINAL for stating rail thermal behaviour backwards. Tooling stated plainly: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) at the first call, Firecrawl search returned HTTP 401 (unauthenticated), and Mojeek/DuckDuckGo/Brave result pages returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so every source below was reached through the Exa web_search_exa MCP tool. (1) M. N. Amster, 'Hydraulic Model Investigation of Miter Gate Operation' (ASCE, doi 10.1061/taceat.0005789): each leaf swings about a vertical axis near its downstream quoin end so that the upstream miter ends meet at the lock centre line; 'In supporting a water load, the gate acts as a three-hinged arch, with the two quoin bearings and the miter bearing forming the hinges and the lock walls acting as abutments for the end thrust.' (2) B. Eick, M. D. Smith, T. B. Fillmore, 'Feasibility of discontinuous quoin blocks for USACE miter gates' (ERDC, doi 10.21079/11681/33490): the quoin 'is intended to facilitate the transfer of hydrostatic load through bearing pressure against the concrete lock wall'; the boundary conditions are 'intended to facilitate a three-hinged arch-like behavior, with the water pressure on the gate being transferred into the lock chamber wall through axial compression of the horizontal girders'. (3) T. B. Fillmore and M. D. Smith, 'Behavior of Flexible Pintles for Miter Gates' (ASCE, doi 10.1061/(asce)ww.1943-5460.0000653) - the decisive source for this item's direction: 'USACE assumes that horizontally framed miter gates thrust into lock chamber walls under hydraulic head. However, in many gates the bottom hinge, a fixed pintle, interrupts this thrusting action by taking a portion of the load itself. As the fixed pintle is not designed for such loading, the resulting high pintle stresses significantly reduce pintle life.' The proposed remedies are free, rocking and elastomeric pintles, i.e. MORE freedom at the foot so the gate can 'fully thrust into the wall'. A fixed foot is the fault condition, not the design. (4) 'Rehabilitating Canal Locks', Timber Framers Guild / Lancaster (C&O Canal gate replacement, lancotf.com PDF), for the timber-canal version of the same fact: 'When the gates are closed, they meet as a miter pointing upstream. The pressure of the water flowing downstream pushes against the gates; consequently, the higher the water level, the tighter the gates get.' And, on the foot: 'The only attachment points of the lock gates are a cast-iron bearing plate with a 3-in.-diameter pin set into the end grain at the bottom of the quoin post, and a collar around the upper end of the post that is anchored into the top of the masonry wall ... The bearing pin at the bottom of the quoin post is not anchored at all, but simply rests on the stone at the bottom of the canal floor, which allows the gates, when closed, to press more tightly into the masonry quoin. The collar at the top can be tightened or loosened by adjusting metal shims as needed.' (5) Stratford-upon-Avon Local History Society, 'Lock Construction': a Cup set into the main cill, a Pin ('sometimes known as a Pintle') in the bottom of the gate, the Collar round the Heel Post, and cast-iron 'Coins' set into the wall giving 'an excellently flat surface, top to bottom, for the gate to bear against'. (6) canallockgates.co.uk, 'Manufacture of Canal Lock Gates in workshop': heel post connected to a mitre post by rails, heel posts 'rounded by hand', balance beam added last. (7) Britannica, 'mitre gate': 'two leaves, the combined lengths of which exceed the lock width by about 10 percent'; the closure forms 'an angle pointing upstream'. (8) Wikipedia, 'Lock (water navigation)': the pair 'close against each other at an 18 degree angle to approximate an arch against the water pressure on the upstream side'. (9) Canal & River Trust, 'Building lock gates' and Country Life, 'The lock-gate maker': green English and Scottish oak, no two locks alike, measurements taken in imperial. Every directional claim in the passage was checked against these before a word was written: V points upstream, not downstream - confirmed by (4), (7), (8); water closes the joint rather than forcing it - confirmed by (4); leaves together longer than the lock is wide - confirmed by (7); heel post rounded, standing on a pin in a cup in the stone - confirmed by (5), (6); THE PIN IS NOT ANCHORED, AND THAT IS WHAT LETS THE LEAF SEAT ITS HEEL HARDER INTO THE WALL - confirmed explicitly by (4) and, from the failure side, by (3); the push then travels through the leaf into the masonry rather than into the pivot - confirmed by (1), (2), (3); the iron plate lining the recess - confirmed by (5), whose cast-iron 'Coins' give the gate a flat bearing face top to bottom; the collar shimmed - confirmed by (4). One clause is the writer's own framing rather than a sourced rule: that the collar is shimmed 'for hang', i.e. to keep the post upright and the mitre posts meeting true. Source (4) says only that the collar can be tightened or loosened with shims 'as needed', and (5) that the collar retains the gate in position; the passage's reading of what that adjustment is for is presented as the carpenter's, not as a standard, and no figure or tolerance is attached to it.
